--- title: "Case study: Proposition 99 with a known spillover structure" subtitle: "Cao & Dowd's `cd` model on 50 states plus DC, set beside `sar`" --- ```{=html}
Run this walkthrough yourself: ▶ Open in Colab
``` California's 1989 tobacco program can reach other states in two ways. Smokers can cross into Arizona, Nevada or Oregon to buy cheaper cigarettes, which is *leakage*. And twelve states passed tobacco-control laws of their own in the following years, which is *policy contamination*. Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller dropped the twelve from the donor pool. Cao and Dowd keep every state and let the exposed ones carry their own effects instead. This page fits that design with the [`cd` model](models/cd.qmd), reads the direct effect and the spillovers, and tests both the spillovers and the assumed structure. It then sets the result beside the [`sar` model](models/sar.qmd) fitted to the classic California panel. No MCMC runs for `cd`; the `sar` comparison at the end uses a tutorial-scale chain. ## Load the data `load_california_cd(51)` returns the authors' panel: per-capita cigarette consumption for the 50 states and DC, 1970–2000, with California treated from 1989. Its `affected_units` are the paper's exposed states: the twelve with their own policies, plus Nevada, so all three neighbours are included. ::: {#df962d22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scspill.data import load_california_cd panel = load_california_cd(51) panel.df.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
state year cigs treated
0 AK 1970 121.3 0
1 AK 1971 123.0 0
2 AK 1972 130.0 0
``` ::: ::: ::: {#92045e00 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} panel.affected_units ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ('AK', 'AZ', 'DC', 'FL', 'HI', 'MA', 'MD', 'MI', 'NJ', 'NV', 'NY', 'OR', 'WA') ``` ::: ::: ## Fit ::: {#69b27045 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scspill import SCSPILL result = SCSPILL({**panel.config_kwargs(), "display_graphs": False}).fit() print(f"Average effect on California, 1989-2000: {result.att:.1f} packs per capita") print(f"The same from California's own synthetic control: {result.att_scm:.1f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Average effect on California, 1989-2000: -9.4 packs per capita The same from California's own synthetic control: -10.8 ``` ::: ::: The defaults are the paper's Section 4 definitions: intervals by inverting the P test, and left-inverse critical values. The `cd` fit has one SCM equation per unit, so every state, not just California, has a synthetic control. ::: {#9ebe3ebc .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.plot(kind="full", display=False); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` findfont: Failed to find font weight medium, now using 400. findfont: Failed to find font weight medium, now using 400. findfont: Failed to find font weight medium, now using 400. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![California against its synthetic control, with the 95% interval of the direct effect after 1989.](prop99-spillovers_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-2.png){width=706 height=496} ::: ::: ## The direct effect ::: {#b9360628 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} ca = result.effect_ci["CA"].assign( estimate=result.effects_panel["CA"], p_value=result.pointwise_p_values["CA"] ) ca.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The effect is indistinguishable from zero in the first years. With 19 pre-treatment years the smallest attainable P value is $1/19 \approx 0.053$, so the 1990–1992 estimates sit just short of the 5% threshold. From 1993 the effect is significant and keeps growing. The paper reads the slow start as consistent with addiction: consumption adjusts gradually to the tax. ## The spillovers ::: {#a3a586eb .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.plot(kind="spillover", display=False); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` findfont: Failed to find font weight medium, now using 400. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Direct effect on California and the spillover on every exposed state, with 95% intervals.](prop99-spillovers_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-2.png){width=1357 height=1025} ::: ::: Nevada is the cleanest read: it had no tobacco law of its own in the 1990s, so its spillover is leakage rather than contamination. ::: {#e1f438e9 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} nv = result.effect_ci["NV"].assign( estimate=result.effects_panel["NV"], p_value=result.pointwise_p_values["NV"] ) nv.round(2).head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Nevada's consumption rises by roughly 15 and 27 packs per capita in the first two years, and the effect then fades. That is what cross-border buying predicts: smokers adapt, and later tax increases elsewhere narrow the price gap. **Is there any spillover at all?** Test that every exposed state's effect is zero, year by year: ::: {#e10653a5 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd no_spillover = np.eye(len(result.unit_labels))[1:] # every unit except California pd.DataFrame( { t: { "statistic": result.test_hypothesis(no_spillover, period=t).statistic, "p_value": result.test_hypothesis(no_spillover, period=t).p_value, "reject": result.test_hypothesis(no_spillover, period=t).reject, } for t in result.effects_panel.index } ).T.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Is the structure right? Everything above assumes the 13 exposed states are the only ones affected. The $\kappa_A$ test checks that: the part of each post-treatment residual that the structure cannot explain should look like the pre-treatment residuals. ::: {#6433f069 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.plot(kind="kappa", display=False); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` findfont: Failed to find font weight medium, now using 400. findfont: Failed to find font weight medium, now using 400. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The kappa_A structure test by year against its 95% critical value.](prop99-spillovers_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-2.png){width=695 height=477} ::: ::: It rejects in every year after 1989. This is a real warning. Something moved after 1989 that the 13-state structure does not capture: national anti-smoking trends, other states' policies, or spillovers on states assumed clean. Comparing candidate structures on the same fit shows that the paper's choice still fits best among the obvious alternatives. A structure that nests another always fits at least as well, so this ranks the alternatives rather than validating the choice. ::: {#597c2d0e .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} choice = result.select_structure_by_kappa( { "paper (13 states, per unit)": {"affected_units": list(panel.affected_units)}, "13 states, one shared spillover": { "spillover_structure": "homogeneous", "affected_units": list(panel.affected_units), }, "neighbours only": {"affected_units": ["AZ", "NV", "OR"]}, "no spillovers": {"affected_units": []}, } ) choice.statistics.round(1).sort_values() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` paper (13 states, per unit) 198.5 neighbours only 218.5 13 states, one shared spillover 222.3 no spillovers 224.3 Name: kappa_A (v3), dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ## How much could a missed spillover matter? If $p$ of the states assumed clean received spillovers of at most $\bar\alpha$, the bias of California's effect is bounded linearly in $\bar\alpha$ (Section 5.2.2 of the paper). The spillover-aware estimator's bound grows far more slowly than that of a synthetic control built only from the clean states: ::: {#ea510e8f .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.plot(kind="sensitivity", display=False); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Worst-case bias of California's effect under p = 1, 2 missed spillovers.](prop99-spillovers_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=695 height=477} ::: ::: ::: {#14942e6f .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} sens = result.cd.sensitivity largest = result.effects_panel["CA"].max() for p in (1, 2): c_sp, c_pd = sens.coefficients(p) print( f"p = {p}: a missed spillover of {largest / c_sp:.2f} packs could account for " f"California's largest estimate ({largest:.2f}); " f"{largest / c_pd:.2f} for the pure-donor SCM." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` p = 1: a missed spillover of 17.07 packs could account for California's largest estimate (3.71); 6.73 for the pure-donor SCM. p = 2: a missed spillover of 9.66 packs could account for California's largest estimate (3.71); 5.33 for the pure-donor SCM. ``` ::: ::: These are the break-even points the paper highlights in its Figure 3: 17.07 for one missed state and 9.66 for two. ## The 41-state specification The authors' repository also drops the ten policy states that do not border California, leaving Arizona, Nevada and Oregon as the only exposed controls: ::: {#2a217490 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} r41 = SCSPILL({**load_california_cd(41).config_kwargs(), "display_graphs": False}).fit() pd.DataFrame( {"51 states": result.effects_panel["CA"], "41 states": r41.effects_panel["CA"]} ).round(2).T ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}

41 states -0.97 4.18 -4.83 -4.52 -8.55 -8.94 -13.96 -14.16 -15.94 -15.97 -20.24 -16.82
``` ::: ::: ## `cd` and `sar`, side by side The [Get started](get-started.qmd) page fits `sar` to the classic panel. The two analyses differ in more than the model, so read the comparison with care: | | `cd` (this page) | `sar` (Get started) | |---|---|---| | Panel | Cao & Dowd: 50 states + DC | Abadie et al.: 39 states (the 12 policy states dropped) | | Outcome | per-capita consumption (`cigs`) | per-capita sales (`cigsale`) | | Treated from | 1989 | 1988 | | Spillover assumption | free effects on 13 named states | one intensity $\rho$ through rook contiguity | | Inference | P tests from the pre-treatment residuals | Bayesian posterior | ::: {#46085204 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} from scspill.data import load_california sar = SCSPILL( {**load_california().config_kwargs(), "m_iter": 4000, "burn": 2000, "seed": 42, "display_graphs": False} ).fit() print(f"sar: ATT {sar.att:.1f} (95% CrI [{sar.att_ci[0]:.1f}, {sar.att_ci[1]:.1f}]), " f"rho {sar.rho_hat:.2f}") print(f"cd: ATT {result.att:.1f} (no interval for the average)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sar: ATT -17.1 (95% CrI [-23.0, -11.0]), rho 0.37 cd: ATT -9.4 (no interval for the average) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cab6eefb .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) years = result.effects_panel.index ax.fill_between(years, result.effect_ci["CA"]["lower"], result.effect_ci["CA"]["upper"], alpha=0.2, color="#1f77b4") ax.plot(years, result.effects_panel["CA"], "o-", color="#1f77b4", label="cd (51 units, from 1989)") t0 = sar.inputs.T0 sar_years = sar.inputs.time_labels[t0:] gap = sar.inputs.Y0[t0:] - sar.effects_detail.cf_mean[t0:] ax.fill_between(sar_years, sar.inputs.Y0[t0:] - sar.effects_detail.cf_upper[t0:], sar.inputs.Y0[t0:] - sar.effects_detail.cf_lower[t0:], alpha=0.2, color="crimson") ax.plot(sar_years, gap, "s-", color="crimson", label="sar (39 states, from 1988)") ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8) ax.set_xlabel("Year") ax.set_ylabel("Effect on California (packs per capita)") ax.legend(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![California's direct effect under the two models, each with its own sample and 95% band.](prop99-spillovers_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-1.png){width=671 height=394} ::: ::: The models agree that the program cut consumption and that the cut grew over the decade. They disagree about Nevada: ::: {#355c20c5 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame( { "cd: spillover on NV": result.effects_panel["NV"].loc[1989:1992], "sar: spillover on Nevada": sar.spillover_panel["Nevada"].loc[1989:1992], } ).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
cd: spillover on NV sar: spillover on Nevada
1989 14.96 -3.45
1990 26.86 -3.81
1991 3.82 -5.04
1992 -1.62 -4.67
``` ::: ::: `cd` leaves the size and sign of each spillover free, and finds Nevada's consumption *rising*: leakage. `sar` routes every spillover through one intensity $\rho$ applied to California's own outcome. Its estimate here is positive, so a fall in California is passed on as a fall in its neighbours. A negative $\rho$ could express leakage, but the one intensity governs every channel at once, and in this sample the data put it above zero. Neither answer is "the" answer. The two models make different assumptions, so running both shows how much the conclusion depends on the spillover assumption. ## Notes on this application - Arizona and Oregon passed tobacco taxes of their own in 1994 and 1996, so their later "spillovers" mix leakage with their own policies. The paper says the same. - The `cd` intervals come from 19 pre-treatment residuals. That limits the smallest attainable P value to $1/19$, and it makes the leave-one-period-out references (`reference_mode="leave_one_period_out"`) noticeably wider. - The [replication article](articles/cd-replication.qmd) shows the authors' published numbers reproduced, with the settings of their application code.
